approachQuestion.prompt: An inventory is represented by nested lists. Each entry is either an integer or another list; empty lists are allowed. Return the sum of every integer at every nesting level. Example 1: [2,[5,[]],-3] returns 4. Example 2: [[],[7]] returns 7. Example 3: [] returns 0.
constraints: The input is a finite, acyclic nested-list structure.
There are n total list and integer entries, with 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000.
The maximum list nesting depth is h, with 0 ≤ h ≤ 10000.
Each integer is in [-1000000000,1000000000]; the sum fits in signed 64-bit.
Return one integer; do not modify the input.

options.text: For an integer entry, return its value. For a list, start with zero and add the recursively computed result of each child; an empty list therefore returns zero.
options.feedback: The result contract has a direct base case for integer entries and a neutral starting value for lists, including empty lists.

options.text: Use an explicit stack of entries, add integers when removed, and push children of each list.
options.feedback: This iterative traversal also visits every entry and handles empty lists; it is an equally valid optimal method.

options.text: Add integer entries directly and ignore entries that are lists.
options.feedback: Nested integers contribute too. For [[4]], this returns 0 instead of 4.

options.text: For each list, repeatedly remove its first child and recursively process the shortened remainder.
options.feedback: This mutates the input and can repeatedly shift list elements. The task forbids mutation; for [1,[2]] it also risks dropping the nested value if only integer children are accumulated.

feedback.reason: A helper summarizes exactly one entry.
details: Define the helper to return the sum represented by one entry. An integer returns itself. A list returns the sum of the helper results for its children, starting from zero; this makes an empty list return zero. Apply the helper once to the outer list.

A helper summarizes exactly one entry. Empty lists contribute zero, and parent lists add child summaries without flattening the structure. Active nesting depth, rather than total list count, determines simultaneous call frames.

“For an integer entry, return its value. For a list, start with zero and add the recursively computed result of each child; an empty list therefore returns zero.”: The result contract has a direct base case for integer entries and a neutral starting value for lists, including empty lists.

“Use an explicit stack of entries, add integers when removed, and push children of each list.”: This iterative traversal also visits every entry and handles empty lists; it is an equally valid optimal method.
“Add integer entries directly and ignore entries that are lists.”: Nested integers contribute too. For [[4]], this returns 0 instead of 4.

“For each list, repeatedly remove its first child and recursively process the shortened remainder.”: This mutates the input and can repeatedly shift list elements. The task forbids mutation; for [1,[2]] it also risks dropping the nested value if only integer children are accumulated.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the recursive-list-sum method, let n be the total number of entries and h the maximum nesting depth. Choose its worst-case time and auxiliary-space costs. The input structure and returned integer are excluded from auxiliary space; active call frames are included.

feedback.reason: Visit every entry once while retaining only the active nesting path.
details: Each integer is visited once, and each list contributes one call frame per active nesting level. Empty structures still return zero.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The traversal visits each entry once, but frames from completed sibling branches are released. Only the currently active nesting path remains on the call stack.
“O(n²) time, O(h) auxiliary space”: The method does not rescan earlier siblings; each entry is handled once.
“O(h) time, O(h) auxiliary space”: The depth bounds simultaneous calls, but every entry must still be visited to include its integer in the sum.
